attack_surfaces.operation: unbounded stack buffer write (gets) into 0x70-byte buffer at rbp-0x70
attack_surfaces.reason: gets() performs no length validation; attacker-controlled input overflows the 0x70-byte stack buffer, overwriting saved rbp (at offset 0x70) and return address (at offset 0x78). No stack canary present, so overflow is not detected. NX enabled so direct shellcode on stack is not executable, but ROP is viable. This is the primary attack surface for S2.

attack_surfaces.operation: stdout (fd 1) and stderr (fd 2) are closed before vuln returns
attack_surfaces.reason: After the overflow, stdout and stderr are closed, meaning any post-exploitation output via puts/printf/write(1,...) will fail. This constrains information leakage and exfiltration strategies. S2 should consider this when evaluating exploit routes (e.g., may need to reopen fd 1 or use a different fd for output, or use one-shot techniques that do not require stdout).

attack_surfaces.operation: ret instruction at 0x401238 returns to attacker-controlled address
attack_surfaces.reason: With return address overwritten at offset 0x78 from buffer start, and no PIE (fixed addresses) + no canary, ROP chain can be constructed using gadgets from the binary (0x400000 range) and/or libc (if base can be leaked or brute-forced). CET SHSTK/IBT is marked enabled in ELF but enforcement depends on kernel/hardware support at runtime (UNKNOWN).

No RPATH/RUNPATH in binary; only NEEDED library is libc.so.6
vuln (0x401205): sub rsp,0x70; lea rax,[rbp-0x70]; gets(rax); close(1); close(2); leave; ret
gets() performs no bounds checking on input length
Stack buffer in vuln is 0x70 (112) bytes; saved rbp at [rbp] is 0x70 bytes from buffer start; return address at [rbp+8] is 0x78 (120) bytes from buffer start
No stack canary in vuln (no canary found in binary; vuln prologue has no canary load/check)
vuln calls close(1) and close(2) after gets(), closing stdout and stderr before function returns
GOT is writable (Partial RELRO); .got.plt at 0x404000, .got at 0x403ff0
PLT entries: alarm@plt 0x401070, close@plt 0x401080, gets@plt 0x401090, setvbuf@plt 0x4010a0
libc key offsets: system 0x58750, execve 0xef030, gets 0x87160, puts 0x87cc0, open 0x11b250, read 0x11bb80, write 0x11c690, environ 0x20ad58, /bin/sh string 0x1cb42f
probe_io with input 'AAAA' produced no output, consistent with vuln closing stdout/stderr after gets
alarm(60) is set in init, so the process will receive SIGALRM after 60 seconds (anti-hang protection)
Offset from start of gets buffer to return address = 0x70 (buffer) + 0x8 (saved rbp) = 0x78 (120 bytes). 120 bytes of padding reach the return address.
Since No PIE + No Canary + writable GOT, the binary is amenable to ROP using fixed-address gadgets. libc addresses require either a leak or brute force (ASLR).

CET (SHSTK/IBT) is marked in ELF but actual enforcement depends on kernel + CPU support at runtime; if enforced, shadow stack would detect return-address overwrite and IBT would require endbr64 at indirect call targets. Enforcement status is UNKNOWN without runtime confirmation.

ldd showed libc at 0x7e3deefd5000 in one run, suggesting ASLR is active, but ASLR is a kernel setting not a binary property. The libc base address at exploit time is unknown without a leak.
